title: Bike Lanes: Yes or No?

lines.text: Welcome to the Town Hall Hour. Tonight's topic: should the city build more bike lanes? Alex, you start.
I'm in favour. Cycling to work is faster than driving in the morning, and it's much cheaper. I've saved a lot of money since I sold my car.
I understand that, but not everyone can cycle. Some people have to carry heavy tools or take children to school.
That's fair, but if we had safer lanes, more parents would use cargo bikes.
Perhaps. My worry is the cost. Building lanes means closing roads, and shops lose customers when cars can't park outside.
Actually, the café on my street says it has more customers since the bike lane opened.
Maya, would you accept a trial?
Yes, I would. If the council tried one new lane on Park Road, I'd be willing to look at the results.
I'd welcome that. We could count how many people use it.
So, a six-month trial. Thank you both.

lines.text: Welcome to Quick Fire, the quiz where you have to think fast. Our contestant today is Hana. Are you ready?
As ready as I'll ever be!

Correct! Question two. What is the capital city of Australia?
Hmm. I want to say Sydney... no, wait. It's Canberra.
Well done for changing your mind! Question three. How many players does a football team have on the pitch?
Eleven.
Right again. Question four, and it's a hard one. Which animal is the largest on Earth?
I think it's the elephant.
Sorry, that's wrong. The answer is the blue whale.

Don't worry. One last question for the bonus. Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?
Shakespeare!
Correct! So you finish with four points. Congratulations, Hana.

title: Life Without a Commute
focus: Present perfect continuous; advantages and disadvantages

lines.text: Welcome to Work Life. My guest today is Andre, who has been working from home for two years. Andre, how's it going?
Mostly very well, Katie. I've been saving a lot of time because I don't have to commute. Before, I spent nearly two hours a day on the train.
That's a huge difference. What do you do with the extra time?
I've been going for a run every morning, and I've started learning the guitar.
Sounds great. Are there any downsides?
Of course. The biggest problem is loneliness. Some days I don't speak to anyone until the evening.
How do you deal with that?
I work from a café twice a week, and I have a video call with my team every morning.
Any advice for people who are starting to work from home?
Yes. Have a proper workspace, even if it's only a small table. And finish work at a fixed time, otherwise you'll never stop.
Good advice. Thank you, Andre.
My pleasure.

title: Six Months Abroad
focus: Present perfect for experiences; comparing schools

lines.text: Today we're talking to Hiro, an exchange student from Japan who has spent six months at our school. Hiro, how has it been?
It's been fantastic, but also challenging. At first, I couldn't understand people because they spoke so fast.
Has your English improved?
A lot. I've learned that watching films with subtitles helps, but speaking with classmates helps even more.
What's different from school in Japan?
Here, students choose some of their subjects. In my school at home, everyone studies the same ones. Also, we don't wear uniforms here.
Do you miss anything?
Rice, definitely! And my family, of course. But I talk to them on video every Sunday.
What's the best thing you've done here?
Joining the school orchestra. I've never played in a group before, and now I play the violin in front of everyone.
That's wonderful. What will you do when you go home?
I'm going to teach my friends some English songs, and I'd like to come back one day.

title: Photography Class: Using Light
focus: Imperatives; zero and first conditional; advice

lines.text: Welcome to the beginners' photography class. Today we'll talk about light, because it's the most important thing in a photo.
Is a more expensive camera better, Zara?
Not necessarily. A good photographer can take excellent pictures with a phone. What matters is knowing how to use the light.
What time of day is the best?
Early morning and late afternoon. The light is soft and golden then. At midday, the sun is strong, and shadows can look harsh.
What if we only have time at midday?
Then look for shade. If you stand under a tree, the light is softer and your photos look better.
What about taking photos of people?
Always ask first. If someone says no, respect that. And try to take the photo from the same height as your subject.
Why is that?
Because it feels more natural. If you take a photo from above, the person can look small.
That makes sense.
For homework, take five photos at different times of day and bring them next week. We'll compare the light together.
